opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's the question everyone asks first, and honestly it's the right one. The way I think about it is that the platform has to be neutral in the same way a cloud provider is neutral. AWS doesn't care whether you're Netflix or a competitor of Netflix; your data is yours, your workloads are yours, and the trust comes from architecture and contracts, not from good intentions.

So concretely, a few things have to be true. First, a partner's proprietary data, their assay results, their structures, their failed programs, never leaves their control in a way that could benefit someone else. That means strict tenant isolation, and increasingly it means techniques like federated training, where models learn from data that stays inside each company's walls and only gradients or aggregate updates move. Second, the outputs, the molecules you design, the IP you generate, belong to the partner. The platform can't have a quiet claim on the next blockbuster.

Then there's where the shared value actually lives. Pharma companies compete fiercely on targets and chemical matter, but they're surprisingly aligned on the underlying science, things like ADMET prediction, toxicity, how molecules behave in the body. Nobody really wins by having a slightly worse model of hERG liability than their competitor. That's precompetitive territory, and it's where pooling signal, carefully, makes everyone better off. Consortia like MELLODDY showed you can do that across big pharma without anyone leaking crown jewels.

The last piece is that you earn trust slowly. The first partners take a leap, and you have to be boringly rigorous: audits, clear governance, transparency about what the models were trained on. Once a few serious players are in and nothing bad has happened, the network effect starts working for you, because the platform genuinely gets better the more people use it, and staying out starts to cost more than joining.

r001.rationale: The response describes strict tenant isolation and federated training, but does not state that individual pharmaceutical customers use single-tenant deployments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and honestly it's the first thing every pharma partner asks us. The short answer is that neutrality is a feature, not a bug, but you have to earn it structurally, not just say it.

The way I think about it: pharma's IP concerns come down to two things. One is data leakage, meaning their proprietary compound libraries, assay results, target hypotheses, whatever, ending up in a model that then benefits a competitor. The other is attribution, meaning if a model helps design a molecule, who owns it, and can anyone later claim it came from their data.

On the first one, we were pretty deliberate about architecture. Each partner's data sits in an isolated environment. We don't pool it into one giant foundation model that everyone shares. The base models are trained on public and licensed data, and then any fine-tuning or conditioning on a partner's proprietary data happens in their tenant and stays there. There's no gradient flowing back into the shared model. That's a real engineering constraint we live with, and it costs us some capability, but it's the price of trust.

On the second one, we set it up so the partner owns the outputs. We're a platform, not a drug company. We're not building a pipeline of our own that competes with the people using us. That matters a lot more than people expect, because the moment you have your own programs, every partner starts wondering whether their work is informing yours.

And then there's a softer piece, which is that the industry has done this before. CROs, contract manufacturers, even cloud providers all went through a version of this. Twenty years ago nobody would put sensitive data in AWS. Now everyone does, because the controls got good enough and the value was obvious. I think medicine design platforms are at that early stage where the controls have to be visibly over-engineered before people relax.

What's actually interesting is that once you get past the IP conversation, the appetite is huge. These teams want better tools. They're just not willing to trade their crown jewels to get them, and I think that's completely reasonable.

r001.rationale: The response says each pharma partner’s data is isolated in its own tenant and kept out of shared models, presenting those controls as the basis for earning trust despite IP concerns.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is being precise about what’s shared and what’s private. You can have a common platform—the tools and infrastructure for designing medicines—without making a company’s targets, experimental data, or molecules available to anyone else.

For that to work, neutrality has to be more than a promise. The access controls, the contracts, and the business model all have to support it. A partner should know what happens to their data, whether it can be used to improve a model, and who owns the outputs. They shouldn’t have to wonder whether the platform will turn around and compete with them using what it learned from their program.

So I’d think of it as sharing capabilities while keeping programs private. Companies can benefit from better tools without giving up the intellectual property that makes their medicines—and their businesses—distinct.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared tools with private customer programs and strong access, contract, and business safeguards, but it does not mention single-tenant deployments for individual pharmaceutical customers or explain their role in making the platform viable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think neutrality has to be something you can demonstrate through the way the platform works. If a pharma company brings us a proprietary target or a dataset, they need to know exactly who can access it, how it’s being used, and who owns the resulting work. They shouldn’t have to wonder whether their data is improving a competitor’s program.

So you need a clear separation between the shared capabilities of the platform and the proprietary work happening on top of it. You can improve the tools—the infrastructure, the workflows, the methods—while keeping each partner’s data and program-specific intellectual property protected. Any sharing beyond that needs to be explicit and agreed upon.

And the business model has to reinforce that promise. If you’re positioning yourself as a neutral partner while also competing with your customers on their most valuable programs, that creates a real tension. The opportunity is to build something useful enough that companies want to use it, with boundaries clear enough that they feel comfortable bringing their best science.

r001.rationale: The response discusses protecting each partner’s data and program-specific IP through clear boundaries, but it does not mention single-tenant deployments for individual pharmaceutical customers.
